# Abstract {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Satellite-based remote sensing provides a scalable approach to monitoring vegetation management across large areas. In the context of airport safety, reliable records of mowing activities on airfield grasslands are needed to analyse their influence on bird populations and the associated risk of bird strikes. Preceding project work demonstrated that pixel-based machine learning models using Sentinel-2 optical imagery can detect mowing events, but identified two key limitations: dependence on cloud-free acquisitions and spatially fragmented predictions at the pixel level.

This thesis investigates two methodological extensions to address these limitations. First, Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data from the Sentinel-1 mission were integrated as a complementary data source. Both Ground Range Detected (GRD) backscatter and interferometric coherence derived from Single Look Complex (SLC) products were evaluated. Second, spatial postprocessing methods, including morphological filtering, median filtering, and superpixel-based aggregation, were implemented to reduce classification noise. An improved machine learning workflow incorporating refined feature selection, scene-level threshold calibration, and systematic model benchmarking was developed and evaluated against the preceding baseline. The study area is located at Zurich Airport, with ground truth mowing records spanning 2019 to 2023.

The results show that Sentinel-2 optical features remain the dominant predictors of mowing events. The best optical model achieved a test-set F1-Score of 0.923. GRD backscatter features provided no measurable improvement, achieving near-random performance in isolation. Interferometric coherence showed a physically meaningful but weak and season-dependent signal: a statistically significant increase in VH coherence after mowing was observed only during the late growing season, while both polarisations showed negligible or inverted responses during the early and peak seasons. Coherence-only models performed near random, though selective integration of coherence with optical features produced the highest test-set F1-Score within the coherence-eligible subset (0.922). At the operational scene level, the best models achieved F1-Scores of 0.689 and 0.749 on two held-out scenes, nearly doubling the performance of the preceding baseline (0.597 and 0.397 respectively). Scene-level threshold calibration emerged as the single most impactful operational improvement, substantially reducing false positives. Spatial postprocessing contributed only marginal additional gains, as threshold calibration had already addressed the dominant source of classification noise. A standalone prototype notebook was developed and applied to an external site near Lindau, where the model correctly identified known mowing events (recall = 0.995) and avoided false detections on non-grassland surfaces without requiring a land cover mask.

The findings indicate that optical vegetation indices, combined with appropriate threshold calibration, provide a robust basis for automated mowing detection. SAR interferometric coherence offers limited added value for pixel-based classification at this site, though parcel-level or segment-based approaches may yield better results. The primary bottleneck for further development remains the availability of spatially precise and diverse ground truth data.

# Acknowledgments {.unnumbered .unlisted}
I would like to thank my supervisors Nils Ratnaweera, Benjamin Sigrist, and Johann Junghardt for their guidance and feedback throughout this thesis. I am grateful to Zurich Airport and the ZHAW research group from the Institute for Environment and Natural Resources for providing the ground truth data that forms the foundation of this study. I also thank Strickhof for providing additional mowing records near Lindau, which enabled the generalisation test, and Agroscope for their willingness to share data, even though the provided records could not be integrated into the final analysis.

AI-based tools such as Claude were used throughout this project to support code development, particularly for SAR data processing, debugging and text refinement in the written report. 

The cover image is courtesy of NASA, obtained via [Unsplash](https://unsplash.com/de/fotos/blick-auf-erde-und-satellit-yZygONrUBe8?utm_source=unsplash&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=creditShareLink) under their free-use license.
